newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU gas oil stock draw keeps pressure on buyers.
newsitem.headline: EU gas oil stock draw keeps pressure on buyers.

text.p: The fall of European middle distillate oil stocks in September, as evidenced by data released on Wednesday, provided little scope for a weakening of prices in the run-up to winter, traders and analysts said.
"The bottom line is that there is no respite for the market. The figures leave it terribly exposed to the weather," said Geoff Pyne, analyst at UBS.
Middle distillate stocks fell 2.93 million barrels, or 1.0 percent, in September to 283.35 million barrels, Stitching Euroilstock said in its monthly stocks report.
The draw leaves middle distillate inventories even further behind year ago levels.
The year-on-year deficit was 33.47 million barrels, or 10.6 percent, compared with a year-on-year deficit of 25.79 million barrels, or 8.3 percent, at the end of August.
"Distillates (stocks in Europe) are 20 million barrels short of comfort and crude 10 million barrels short. In the U.S., they are also 20 million barrels short of distillate," Pyne said.
Crude stocks in Europe were down 6.13 million barrels to 398.22 million, very similar to last year's levels.
"The draw tempers the build in the U.S. yesterday and, of course, European distillates have been driving the market," said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said on Tuesday distillate stocks in the United States rose by 1.3 million barrels to 113.6 million in the week ending October 4, down 17.1 million on the equivalent week last year.
Traders and analysts expected to see continued gas oil strength, relative to crude, for at least a week until the next release of U.S. stocks data.
"A lot depends on what the API's show next week. Although its supportive of prices, Euroil will be old news by then," said Bogin.

Some observers said high prices have deterred end-users from buying heating oil. Once private stocks are restored to an acceptable level, lower than the historical norm, prices will have to come off -- but many say this is at least a month away.
Traders also said that buyers cannot rely on falling prices despite the backwardation of the gas oil futures market.
"The feeling in Europe is that people will wait to buy. But you have to pay a hefty premium the longer you wait. We're still very bullish the (gas oil) crack," said a trader with one European major.
The strength of diesel prices looked less likely to fade with stocks deemed very tight.
Cargoes arriving from the U.S. have not tended to have a cetane index high enough to suit the average European vehicle, traders say.
"There's less and less 0.05 diesel available now," one said.
"(The shortfall of middle distillates) has undoubtedly been made worse by the 0.05 (percent) sulphur ruling on diesel at the start of this month," Pyne said.
The European Union stipulated that diesel sold from the start of October must have a sulphur content no higher than 0.05 percent, four times less than before.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5004
